Issued at 333 PM CST Tue Nov 24 2026

...Synopsis...

Water vapor satellite imagery reveals broad upper troughing over
the Northern Plains this afternoon. Embedded within this upper
trough are coherent shortwave troughs - one in particular nicely
depicted in water vapor imagery within the central Dakotas. This
feature is driving light snow that has been occurring south of
Highway 2. Despite snow rate and accumulations being light, it
does have the potential to impact travel conditions this
afternoon into evening, including the busier commuting hours.
More details on this found below.

Starting this evening, the upper trough starts to dive 
southeast, pushing snow production away from our area deeper 
into MN. As it continues southeast, the upper trough cuts off
into an upper low, with shortwave ridging on its northern
periphery, with broader southwest/zonal flow aloft in southern
CAN. This nearby southwest flow aloft along with shortwave 
ridging will help conditions stay dry, while also bringing a
southerly wind and perhaps fog into portions of eastern ND
tonight through Wednesday morning. Fog may be dense if it does
form, although confidence is low in whether or not fog actually
does form (or if it stays as a low cloud deck instead of fog).
There is a 40% chance for dense fog west of the Red River 
Valley tonight and Wednesday morning.

This pattern will also trend temperatures toward warmer than
average for mid to late week, including Thanksgiving. Daytime
temperatures are forecast near to above freezing, with overnight
temperatures still falling below freezing.

Around Friday, most ensemble guidance shows a mid level shortwave
trough and attendant surface low pressure moving through 
southern CAN and potentially into ND / MN. At this time, 
majority of forcing associated with this stays within CAN, with
intermittent rain showers in the forecast (rain due to
above freezing temperatures during the wave's passage currently
favored daytime Friday). However, should the wave move further
south and or move through slower, more widespread precipitation
(including snow) may occur. Snow chances will increase if this
wave moves through more during the overnight hours.

While there is the scenario of at least some light snow into our
area Friday/Saturday, the chance of snow is low enough to
maintain messaging that chance for hazardous weather impacts
remains low. This may change in subsequent days as modeled
guidance resolves this feature better.

...Light snow leading to travel impacts during this afternoon/evening
commute...

Widespread light snow falling over much of the area along and
south of Highway 2 (excluding Devils Lake basin) has resulted
in reported road conditions consisting of wet, patchy snow-
covered, and patchy-ice covered. This is due to enough snow to
deposit some moisture, as well as road temperatures at or just
above freezing. Wet roads are likely a result from snow melting
on above freezing roads.

Recent reports of slick roads in Grand Forks and Fargo areas
(especially elevated surfaces like bridges) have proven this
light snow is enough to impact travel conditions. Latest
guidance on road temperatures indicates they are liable to dip
well below freezing by sunset. This could effectively turn wet
roads into icy roads, especially as light snow continues to
fall.

Thus, we have increased messaging potential impact from light
snow to the locally increased traveler timeframe of the 
afternoon and evening commutes.

The potential for impacts is compounded by the fact that this 
is the first snowfall for many within our area.

While there is still uncertainty how long snow will continue to
fall into tonight, there is relatively high confidence snow will
linger through the commute hours.

Lastly - there is a signal for potential freezing drizzle for a
few hours as snow pulls away to the south overnight tonight. 
This may also deposit light icing, further continuing potential
for travel impacts.
